title: Scoped Resource Management

validation.research: Six primary sources: Bjarne Stroustrup’s resource-management/finally FAQ; Stroustrup and Sutter’s C++ Core Guidelines R.1; official Python with-statement, ExitStack, gzip and TemporaryDirectory documentation. Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII) names the C++ object-lifetime idiom; Python explicit context scopes express the same ownership goal without claiming identical destructor semantics. Ownership can transfer or extend beyond an initial lexical block. Wrapping a resource does not establish ownership of its release; GzipFile explicitly leaves a supplied raw file open. Successful-entry registration, reverse dependency unwinding, internal cleanup responsibility of failing entry, exit exception replacement/suppression and release-error limits are source-supported. The archive scenario, size limits, composition, code and diagrams are original teaching material.

runnable_example.verification: Actual article fences executed unchanged. Exact three-line output; invalid type, mutable input, empty and 65-byte inputs reject before any acquisition; empty, ordinary, exact eight-byte output and padded 64-byte compressed input accepted; nine-byte output rejected. Real gzip bad header, CRC and truncated trailer errors propagate. Instrumentation retains real resources and wraps entry/exit seams without replacing article logic or ExitStack. Real decoder close leaves supplied raw open; raw closes before directory removal. All live handles are closed and directories absent before caller observes a result/error. Output remains independent immutable bytes and caller input unchanged; separate calls own distinct directories. A real raw-file open failure releases only directory; injected decoder-construction and failed-entry cases clean prior acquisitions, with entry cleaning its own partial wrapper and no unmatched decoder exit. BaseException body interruption unwinds all successful registrations. Decoder/raw cleanup errors injected after actual close still run remaining exits and replace success; body plus decoder cleanup failure retains BadGzipFile as exception context. Cleanup invocation does not prove release success under arbitrary release errors. No abrupt-process cleanup, rollback, async/background completion, deadline, or decompression CPU/memory security bound is inferred.

example_limits: Original Python archive reader using real TemporaryDirectory, raw file and GzipFile contexts registered in ExitStack. Trusted immutable compressed input is 1–64 bytes; accepted decoded content is 0–8 bytes. A nine-byte sample detects excess output but is not a decompression resource-limit or security sandbox. GzipFile borrows its supplied raw file, so raw ownership is registered separately. Successful acquisitions unwind decoder, raw file, directory before returning independent bytes or propagating an error. Partial setup unwinds only successfully entered contexts; failed entry owns its internal partial cleanup. Cleanup invocation does not guarantee successful release, rollback, durable output, crash recovery or completion of background borrowers. Actual-code verification additionally exercises real malformed-header, CRC and truncated-trailer failures, all input/output byte boundaries, separate successful calls, unchanged caller input, retained real handles proving explicit close, a real missing-file acquisition failure, decoder-construction and failed-entry seams, BaseException body interruption, decoder/raw exit failures injected after actual close, remaining exit execution, and chained body-error context. No general resource-security limit is inferred from a buffered nine-byte read. Abrupt process termination is outside structured exit guarantees.
